name: Avalanche Glacier
approach: From Cold Springs trailhead, traverse via round-the-mountain trail to the southwest side of Mount Adams, approach glacier directly from southwest.
descent: Descend via the south side (South Spur) or the adjacent snowfield.

bivy.name: Cold Springs / South Climb trailhead
bivy.notes: Most South Climb parties sleep here the night before, either to acclimatise a little or to get an alpine start without carrying a camp to the Lunch Counter. Facilities are primitive — a vault toilet, no piped water, no developed fee sites. Access is FR 80 to FR 8040 and then FR 8040-500, roughly eight miles of washboarded and rutted gravel with the last three miles steep, narrow and switchbacked; ordinary cars get up it at low speed but a low-slung vehicle can bottom out, and RVs and trailers should not attempt it. The road generally opens around mid-May and is usually clear of snow by the start of July, so early-season parties should expect to park lower and walk.
bivy.water: Unreliable. Treat this as a dry camp and arrive with water. Small springs and Morrison Creek near the road can be running early in the season and gone by late summer.
bivy.permit: A recreation pass is required to park — Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass, or a day pass; a valid Mt. Adams Climbing Pass parking stub also works between May 1 and Sept 30. Camping here is below the 7,000 ft climbing-pass threshold, so a free self-issued wilderness permit covers you unless you go above that line. Waste bags are usually stocked at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites plus overflow in the parking area; fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Avalanche Glacier high bivy
bivy.notes: Reached by the Round the Mountain trail west from Cold Springs and then up the ridge beside the Avalanche Glacier. Parties usually place camp somewhere above 9,000 ft to shorten summit day.
bivy.water: None; melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Adams Climbing Pass (above 7,000 ft)
bivy.capacity: A few small tent sites on rock and snow benches

bivy.name: Lunch Counter
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the South Climb and effectively the only sheltered ground on the route, a wide rubble bench under Suksdorf Ridge about four miles and 3,700 ft above Cold Springs. It sits anywhere from roughly 9,200 to 9,400 ft because the bench is long and people camp at both ends rather than at one spot. The rock walls left by earlier parties are the whole reason to camp here — wind funnels across the bench and an unprotected tent takes a beating — so plan on repairing a wall rather than finding a perfect one. The summit ridge east of here forms the Yakama Nation boundary; the South Climb stays on Forest Service ground, but do not descend or traverse east off the standard line.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and seasonal. Running meltwater usually appears at the upper end of the bench through early and mid summer, but it is not dependable — in a thin snow year or by late season the bench can be dry, so carry a stove and fuel to melt snow.
bivy.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — this camp is above the 7,000 ft threshold that triggers it between May 1 and Sept 30. Bought through recreation.gov, valid for a single climbing trip; carry it and leave a copy in the windshield. Parking at the South Climb trailhead needs a recreation pass, and the climbing pass parking stub satisfies that within Mt. Adams Wilderness in season. Outside that window or below 7,000 ft, a free self-issued wilderness permit is what applies. Human waste must be packed out in the supplied bags.
bivy.capacity: Large — dozens of parties on summer weekends, spread across a broad bench; scores of pre-built rock windbreaks, though the best-sheltered ones fill first

bivy.name: Morrison Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The fallback camp when the upper road defeats a vehicle or when Cold Springs is full, about three miles below the South Climb trailhead on the same road. The 2012 Cascade Creek fire burned through here, so shade is patchy and there is standing dead timber to consider when choosing a tent spot in wind. Camping here means driving or walking the last steep section to the trailhead in the morning, which costs about an hour but keeps the option open when the road is rough.
bivy.water: Morrison Creek runs beside the camp but is seasonal and can be low or dry by late summer; treat what you take and do not count on it in August or September.
bivy.permit: No climbing pass needed at this elevation — it sits well below the 7,000 ft line. A free self-issued wilderness permit covers travel into Mt. Adams Wilderness from here, and a recreation pass applies at the trailheads above.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites, several strung along the creek

itinerary: Day 1: approach to a high camp near Mad Cat Meadow or Salt Creek. Day 2: alpine start, climb the Avalanche/White Salmon Glaciers to the summit, descend via the South Spur to camp. Day 3: hike out.

name: North Face of the Northwest Ridge
approach: Forest Service Road 2329 from Taklakh Lake area (5.7 miles). Killen Creek Trail (#113) to Pacific Crest Trail junction, then High Camp Trail (#10) to meadow camp at 6,900 ft.
descent: Descend via the North Ridge, or ski/downclimb the same line in favorable conditions.

bivy.name: High Camp (Adams Creek Meadows)
bivy.notes: The base for the north side, reached by the Killen Creek trail from about 4,600 ft to the PCT and then a boot path up to the meadows below the Adams Glacier. Roughly four miles and 2,300 ft of gain, an easy carry compared with the Lunch Counter, and it puts you directly under the glacier's icefall. There is no shelter from wind other than what the rock benches give you, and afternoon weather rolls in fast off the north face. Snow lingers here into July in a heavy year, which affects both the boot track and where you can pitch.
bivy.water: Generally reliable through summer. Meltwater streams from the Adams Glacier snout and small tarns feed the meadows, and Killen Creek runs lower on the approach; filter everything, and expect surface streams to shrink late in a dry season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the Killen Creek trailhead. Note the elevation carefully — at about 6,900 ft this camp sits just under the 7,000 ft threshold, so the camp itself does not require a Cascade Volcano Pass, but any climbing above that line between May 1 and Sept 30 does, so a party heading for the Adams Glacier or North Ridge needs one. Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for trailhead parking. Camp on durable ground and well back from water — this is fragile subalpine meadow.
bivy.capacity: Moderate — open meadow and bench terrain with many dispersed spots; busy in wildflower season but rarely crowded by alpine standards

bivy.name: Adams Glacier moraine bivy
bivy.notes: Parties attacking the Adams Glacier sometimes move above High Camp onto the moraines below the icefall to shorten summit day, with usable ground reported roughly between 7,100 and 7,700 ft depending on which rib and how the moraine has changed. Exact spots shift year to year as the glacier retreats and the moraine slumps, so treat any elevation given for it as approximate and be prepared to camp lower. It is exposed, rockfall from the moraine walls is a real consideration in warm weather, and there is no shelter at all — the trade is a shorter and colder-snow start onto the glacier. Whether the extra carry beats simply starting early from High Camp is argued both ways.
bivy.water: Meltwater from the glacier snout and moraine pools during the day, freezing overnight; workable in warm conditions but not a certainty. Most parties melt snow here rather than depend on running water.
bivy.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — above 7,000 ft, May 1 through Sept 30, single trip, from recreation.gov. Outside that window a free self-issued wilderness permit applies instead. Pack out all human waste.
bivy.capacity: Very small — a few flat gravel or snow platforms for one or two tents; you may have to build a platform

itinerary: Day 1: approach to high camp near Trail Divide or the Adams Glacier basin. Day 2: alpine start, climb the face to the ridge crest and summit, descend via the North Ridge. Day 3: hike out.

name: Avalanche Gulch
approach: From Bunny Flat, follow the trail up through red fir forest to Horse Camp and the stone Sierra Club cabin at about 7,900 ft, which has a spring and camping. Above Horse Camp, follow Olberman's Causeway, a path of laid stones, above tree line, then continue up past Spring Hill and 50/50 Flat into lower Avalanche Gulch. Keep climbing on snow to Helen Lake at about 10,400 ft, a broad flat bench in the gulch and the usual high camp. The lake itself is buried under snow for most of the climbing season.

bivy.name: Horse Camp
bivy.notes: Near the stone Sierra Club cabin just below tree line, with spring water; a small camping fee applies.

bivy.name: Helen Lake
bivy.notes: The usual high camp for a two-day climb: a broad, flat bench in Avalanche Gulch, usually snow-covered and exposed to wind. Above 10,000 ft, so a Summit Pass is required to camp here.

itinerary: Day 1: Bunny Flat to Helen Lake via Horse Camp and Olberman's Causeway, and set up high camp. Day 2: Alpine start from Helen Lake, climb through the Red Banks and over Misery Hill to the summit, then descend to camp, pack up and walk out to Bunny Flat. Single-day parties leave Bunny Flat in the very early hours and climb the whole route in one push.

name: Hurwal Divide Traverse
approach: From Hurricane Creek Trailhead, walk the Hurricane Creek Trail about 1.8 miles to the unsigned, unmaintained Thorp Creek trail on the left (east), in a grassy meadow. Ford Hurricane Creek (cold and fast early in the season), cross the wide cobbled wash of Twin Creek without losing the tread, then climb steep switchbacks through burned forest and blowdown to Thorp Creek Meadows below Sacajawea. Fill up on water here: it is the last reliable source until you are back down at Hurricane Creek.
itinerary: Usually done as a very long single day by fast, experienced scramblers, or as a two- or three-night trip with camps at Thorp Creek Meadows and high on the Hurwal Divide. Day trips should start before first light.

name: Three Sisters Traverse
approach: From the Devils Lake Trailhead (5,450') on the Cascade Lakes Highway, cross the highway and follow the South Sister climbers' trail up through forest. After about 1.5 miles it leaves the trees and crosses a trail junction onto the open plateau below South Sister's South Ridge, which leads straight up to the summit.

bivy.name: Camp Lake
bivy.notes: Below the saddle between South and Middle Sister. Very windy with limited, popular sites. Camp at least 200' from the shore; no campfires.

bivy.name: Timberline below the Hayden Glacier
bivy.notes: Near the foot of the Hayden Glacier moraine on the exit, about 5 miles above Pole Creek; creeks nearby.

itinerary: Leave a car at the Pole Creek Trailhead and drive the other to the Devils Lake Trailhead. Single day: pre-dawn start up South Sister, down its Northwest Ridge, over Middle Sister south to north, then North Sister, and out to Pole Creek. Two days: camp near Camp Lake or the Hayden Glacier timberline between the peaks (overnight permit required), leaving North Sister for the second morning while the snow is firm.

name: South Ridge (Scatter Lake)
approach: From Twisp, drive Twisp River Road west approximately 22-24 miles to the Scatter Creek/Scatter Lake trailhead (~3,100-3,200 ft), about 50 yards past the Slate Creek Trail junction sign. Follow the Twisp River Trail (#440) a few hundred feet to the Scatter Creek Trail (#427) and take it through timber alongside Scatter Creek for about 4.2-4.5 miles to alpine Scatter Lake (~7,047-7,100 ft).
descent: Reverse the ridge and talus slope to Scatter Lake; scree-skiing the talus is a fast, common way down in dry conditions.

bivy.name: Scatter Lake basin
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Abernathy Peak and it sits directly under both of its routes. From Twisp the Twisp River road runs about 22 miles, turning off on an unpaved spur immediately after the Scatter Creek crossing; pavement ends several miles before that. The trail is a hard 4.6 miles with roughly 3,800 ft of gain to a lake just under 7,000 ft, so most parties either take the whole day to reach it or accept a long day out and back. From camp the South Ridge is the straightforward line, a steep loose scree slog above the lake, and the North Ridge is reached by working around the basin. The whole face above the lake has a southern aspect and is normally snow free from early July; before that, expect firm snow in the gully and an ice axe is not optional. Late September and the first week of October is the classic window here for the larch, and it is also when the basin is busiest. Bring what you need for a cold dry camp: this is east-side country, the nights are colder than the drive up suggests, and there is no shelter of any kind.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and Scatter Creek is beside the trail for most of the climb. This is one of the more reliable water situations in the zone.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit is needed to hike or camp on the Forest Service side of this range. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Scatter Creek trailhead. Fill in the trailhead register where one is present. Firewood is scarce and the lakeshore vegetation is fragile, so treat this as a stove-only camp regardless of whether a formal fire ban is posted, and expect an actual east-side fire restriction from midsummer into September in most years.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent sites around the lake, plus a stock camp in the meadow about a mile below it. Small basin, and it fills on larch weekends in late September and early October.

itinerary: Long day trip from the trailhead (roughly 9-11 miles round trip with ~5,100-5,400 ft of gain), or an easier overnight with a camp at Scatter Lake before a lighter summit push.

name: Accidental Discharge (East Face)
approach: One approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route over Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching South Peak. That way arrives on the Chickamin Glacier on the west side of the crest, while this route starts out of the moat of the Blue Glacier on the east side; the approach from the east up Agnes Creek puts you on that side directly. Either way this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.
descent: No descent specific to this route has been published. What is documented is that the east face rises straight out of the Blue Glacier, and that the established way off the South Peak drops back to that same glacier: roughly 35 m of rappel north off the summit, then a rappel east onto the ice. Treat that as the working descent until better beta exists. A recorded rappel to the Blue Glacier off this summit hung free over a moat, so assume a gap at the bottom, budget anchor material, and do not count on fixed gear. Given the loose rock reported on the climb, rappelling the line of ascent is a poor idea.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road has been closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. On top of that, the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) closes the Downey Creek Trailhead, the Downey Creek Trail and the Bachelor Creek Trail from August 15 through December 31, 2026, unless rescinded sooner. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

itinerary: Day 1: drive to Downey Creek TH and hike ~12-13 mi / ~5,700 ft gain via Bachelor Creek to an Itswoot Ridge camp. Day 2: ~3 mi / ~2,500 ft further to a high camp near the Dome-Chickamin col (~8,500 ft). Day 3: reach the base of the East Face on the Blue Glacier and climb; return to high camp. Days 4-5: reverse the approach.

name: South Ridge (via Asa Peak NE Ridge)
approach: From High Bridge in Stehekin, follow the PCT/Agnes Creek Trail south roughly 8-10 miles (about 5.2 hours to a Swamp Creek-area camp) to the Agnes Creek/Spruce Creek confluence. Cross Agnes Creek on a log, then Spruce Creek on another log shortly after, and climb steeply northwest off-trail through brush, talus, and slabs to a camp near Upper Blue Basin (~5,000 ft), then continue to a high camp near Icy-Spruce Pass (~6,760 ft) for the summit push.
descent: Downclimb the final scramble, then reverse the roped pitches/chimney with 3 rappels to the upper gully, and descend the ~1,400-ft east-facing snow couloir (flukes/running belays) back to the south col before reversing the ridge traverse to camp.
itinerary: Day 1: High Bridge to a Swamp Creek-area camp (~8.5 mi PCT). Day 2: cross Agnes and Spruce Creeks, climb to Upper Blue Basin camp (~5,000 ft). Day 3: move to a high camp near Icy-Spruce Pass (~6,760 ft). Day 4: summit push via the south ridge and chimney crux (reported ~10.6 hr up, ~8.8 hr down); return to high camp. Day 5: hike out to High Bridge.

name: Round Mountain Trail (Standard Route)
approach: From Leavenworth, drive US Highway 2 west approximately 17.4-17.7 miles (or from Stevens Pass, drive east about 18 miles) to just past the Nason Creek Rest Area. Turn north (right heading west / left heading east) onto the unsigned Butcher Creek Road, Forest Road 6910 -- watch for the turn on a curve with fast highway traffic. Follow FR 6910 (good gravel) for about 4.5 miles, then turn onto spur FR 6910-170 and continue roughly 0.1-0.25 mile to the Round Mountain Trailhead.
descent: Descend the same trail: Nason Ridge Trail #1583 back to the Round Mountain Trail #1529 junction, then down Round Mountain Trail to the trailhead.

bivy.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.

bivy.name: Alpine Lookout — day use only, no overnight
bivy.notes: The lookout itself: you may walk to it and, if it is staffed and the lookout is willing, speak to whoever is on duty, but you may not stay in it or expect shelter from it. Plan the day accordingly and do not treat the building as a bail-out option in bad weather. The approach follows the Round Mountain trail for about a mile and a half to the ridge crest trail, then runs along the ridge with repeated ups and downs for another five miles to the lookout, roughly ten miles round trip with about 2,600 feet of gain — two thirds of that gain in the first two miles and the rest scattered along the crest. The approach can also be made from the Merritt Lake end, which is the only version of this trip that passes water. Mountain goats are frequently around the lookout and are habituated enough to approach people; keep well clear of them, never feed them, and be careful about salt on packs and clothing. Anyone needing to sleep before or after should plan on Merritt Lake to the west or the drive-in campgrounds down at the highway.
bivy.water: None at all, and none for the last several miles of trail in either direction. There is one seasonal spring close to the Round Mountain trailhead that runs early in the year and cannot be relied on; past it the trail is dry the whole way. From the west, the last water is Merritt Lake, about three miles back. Carry everything.
bivy.permit: A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is required at the Round Mountain trailhead. No wilderness permit, no quota, no lottery — none of Nason Ridge is designated wilderness. Campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the surrounding forest is dry enough that fire restrictions are near-permanent through the summer, which is rather the point of the building on the summit.
bivy.capacity: None for the public. This is an active Forest Service fire lookout, staffed through the summer fire season, and it is NOT available to sleep in, not rentable, and not one of the lookouts in this state that take overnight visitors. Treat it as a staffed workplace: the summit is a fine place to stand, and the building is somebody's post. There is no established campsite at the lookout either, and the ground around it is narrow open ridge crest.

itinerary: Single long day: trailhead to lookout is commonly done as a ~9.6-10.2 mile round trip with roughly 4-7 hours of hiking depending on pace and side-trips; some parties camp along Nason Ridge (e.g. near Rock Lake or Crescent Lake, accessed via side trails) to split it into an overnight.

name: Finger of Fatwa
approach: Most parties start at the Andrews Creek trailhead (trail 504) at the edge of the Pasayten Wilderness. Follow the valley about four miles to the usual first camp in the burned section, cross Andrews Pass, then join the Boundary Trail to Upper Cathedral Lake; the whole trip is roughly 17 miles with about 4,800 ft of gain. Camp near the lake, which fills a boulder-strewn basin right under the north face of Amphitheater Mountain. Looking up from the shore, the Middle Finger Buttress is the one to the right of the Ka'aba Buttress; walk around the shore and scramble about 15 minutes up to the base of Middle Finger Buttress, where the route starts on the face directly above the lake.
descent: As for Middle Finger Buttress routes: hike east along the ridge crest to the small col southwest of the North Ridge, then descend the 3rd-class gully on the north slope.

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

bivy.name: Andrews Pass
bivy.notes: The natural first-night stop if you leave the trailhead in the afternoon, roughly twelve miles up the drainage and about the halfway mark to the Cathedral basin. Everything below here is burn — the lower Andrews Creek drainage has been through repeated fire and the trail was closed for years after it, so expect open, hot walking with little shade and standing dead timber that comes down in wind. Blowdown volume in the burn varies a lot year to year and is worth asking the Methow Valley district about before committing to a schedule. Breaking the walk here rather than pushing to the lakes makes a big difference to how the second day goes.
bivy.water: Streams on both sides of the pass, and the trail below it runs genuinely boggy in places early in the season. This is the last stretch of the approach where water is easy; reliability drops off through August and September.

name: Northeast Couloir
approach: From the Stuart Lake/Mountaineer Creek trailhead, follow the Stuart Lake Trail past the Colchuck Lake junction (do not turn off), then leave the trail to bushwhack and cross Mountaineer Creek (a notorious slide-alder slope is best avoided via nearby talus). Snow is typically encountered around 4,700 ft; continue to the base of the north face couloir. After leaving the Stuart Lake Trail near 4,700 ft, follow the cairned boot path through the boulder field and avoid climbing too high there, or you drift toward the Sherpa and Stuart side.
descent: One rappel from the upper rock band to a ledge on the southeast face, then two or three single-rope rappels down the gully east of the couloir’s top to the snow, and a long glissade down the Colchuck Glacier to Colchuck Lake and out the Colchuck Lake trail.

bivy.name: Argonaut north basin bivies, below the Colchuck-Argonaut col
bivy.notes: From the bench in Mountaineer Creek the valley forks around 4,800 feet; take the easternmost fork and climb toward the col between Colchuck and Argonaut, and the flat ground in the basin at roughly this height is the high camp for the Northeast Couloir and the Northwest Arete. It puts the foot of the couloir within an easy start, which matters because that line is a snow route best climbed cold and early. The basin is rocky, open and exposed, with no shelter of any kind, so bring a real bivy sack or a tent rather than counting on finding a nook. The travel from the forks up is off-trail on moraine and slabs and takes longer than the distance suggests. Note that this camp serves only Argonaut's north side; the South Face and Southeast Ridge are approached from Ingalls Creek and there is no reasonable way to link the two in a day.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and meltwater off the permanent snow below the col, reliable in early and midsummer and unreliable late; by September expect to melt snow or carry up from the forks lower down
bivy.permit: Approached from the Stuart Lake trailhead, so the same unresolved boundary question applies as at the Mountaineer Creek bench. Assume the Stuart Zone overnight permit is required May 15 to October 31 unless the Wenatchee River Ranger District tells you otherwise. Day climbing needs only the free self-issued wilderness permit. No fires, no dogs.
bivy.capacity: Several small gravel and slab platforms scattered through the upper basin; two or three parties fit if they spread out, and none of the spots is large

itinerary: Often climbed as one long day, or with a bivy on the approach; one trip report logged 15 hours car-to-car.

name: Austera Peak
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From camp, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) climbing to the high camp on the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier below Eldorado's east ridge. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Important — this route is not on Eldorado Peak itself, despite being filed under the same area: from the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp (~7,600ft), continue traversing the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti col; Tepeh Towers are passed along this same glacier traverse, and Austera Peak requires further travel across the Klawatti Glacier (including a short rappel from the col) beyond Klawatti Peak — meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado.
descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a different cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A bear canister is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

itinerary: Day 1: hike Cascade River Road/Eldorado Creek trail and Eldorado Glacier to East Ridge high camp (~7,600 ft), 5-6 hrs. Day 2: traverse the glacier system to Austera Peak and back (~4 hrs one-way plus summit climbing), optionally continuing to Klawatti/Primus as part of the broader Isolation/Inspiration Traverse. Day 3: descend to the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek / Cascade River Road TH

name: East Face
approach: No approach is known for this route. The only fixed reference point is the Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft, reached by turning north off US Highway 2 at milepost 42 in Baring onto Barclay Creek Road (FS Road 6024), crossing the railroad tracks, bearing left at the fork 0.2 miles up, and driving roughly 4.3-4.5 miles of gravel. From there, Barclay Creek Trail 1055 runs 2.2 miles up the valley to Barclay Lake beneath the north side. Reaching the east face requires either continuing up the Barclay Creek drainage past the lake and gaining the east-side slopes off-trail, or approaching over the mountain via the standard northwest-ridge climbers' path and traversing around. Neither is described, and a reconnaissance trip to identify the line and its base is strongly advised before committing to a climbing day.
descent: Undocumented. Assume you will either rappel the route or top out and descend the standard northwest-ridge / base-jumper trail to the west.
itinerary: A single long day from the Barclay Lake trailhead, with a strong case for splitting it across two: one trip to find the face and the base of the line, and a second to climb it. There is no established bivy site on the east side; camping at Barclay Lake on Trail 1055 is the nearest practical option.

waypoints.name: Barclay Lake Trailhead (end of FS Road 6024)

name: Northwest Ridge
approach: Drive US Highway 2 to milepost 42 in Baring — the turnoff is directly across from Der Baring Store — and turn north onto Barclay Creek Road (Forest Service Road 6024). Cross the railroad tracks immediately, and about 0.2 miles up bear left at the fork. Follow the gravel road roughly 4.3-4.5 miles to the Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft; there is parking for about 20 cars, a vault toilet and picnic tables, but no potable water. Do not start on Barclay Creek Trail 1055. Instead, walk about a third of a mile up the overgrown, abandoned logging road that continues uphill from the parking area, past the toilet. At the first creek crossing look right for a cairn marking the start of the climbers' path — you will cross the creek twice, which is a useful confirmation you are on the right track. From there the path climbs relentlessly and directly up the forested north/west side of the mountain, with pink flagging that may or may not be present, a short heavily eroded class-3 step where hand lines have been reported, and several places where the trail braids. Gain the ridge crest near 4,000 ft, follow it east for roughly a mile, then descend below the cliff bands on the south side, cross the wooded gully, and traverse up into the talus basin at about 4,900 ft. Navigation is straightforward from the basin onward.
descent: Reverse the ascent route: back down the notch gully into the basin, along the ridge, and down the steep forested climbers' path to the logging road and trailhead.

bivy.name: Money Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

bivy.name: Basin under the twin summits
bivy.notes: The boulder-and-heather basin under the north and south summits, reached just before the final gully to the notch. The only flat ground on the route; parties carry water.
bivy.water: Snow patches early season only; often dry by late summer
bivy.permit: No overnight permit required
bivy.capacity: A few tents on heather and boulder flats

itinerary: Day trip. Most parties do it car to car in a long day, leaving Seattle early. There is no practical high camp on the route itself; if you want to break it up, camp at Barclay Lake (2.2 easy miles on Trail 1055) the night before and drive/walk back to the climbers' path start in the morning — though the lake is on a different approach and this adds mileage rather than saving it. Camping at the trailhead the night before is the simpler option.

waypoints.name: Barclay Lake Trailhead (end of FS Road 6024)

name: Oatmeal Man
approach: From US Highway 2 at milepost 42 in the town of Baring (directly across from Der Baring Store), turn north onto Barclay Creek Road, Forest Service Road 6024, cross the BNSF railroad tracks and bear left at the fork about 0.2 miles up. Follow FS 6024 roughly 4.3–4.5 miles of gravel to the Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft, where there is parking for roughly 20 cars, a vault toilet and picnic tables but no potable water. Walk Barclay Creek Trail 1055 east up the valley — it is a gentle, well-graded 2.2 miles to Barclay Lake at about 2,420 ft, directly under the wall. The footlog over Barclay Creek about 1.2 miles in has been removed, so expect to ford the creek until it is replaced; check current trail status. The north face rises straight out of the lake basin: 3,703 vertical feet from the lake to the summit in only half a mile of horizontal distance. Leave the trail near the lake and fight up the steep forested and brushy hillside beneath the wall — the first ascent of this face in 1960 found the first 1,000 feet to be exactly that kind of brush-and-forest struggle to reach a camp below the couloirs, and nothing about that terrain has improved since. There is no maintained climbers' path to the base of the main-peak wall (the fixed lines and boot track that exist on this mountain belong to the Dolomite Tower approach, which breaks off the trail well before the lake and heads up a different drainage). Allow several hours from the car to the base and expect wet vegetation, blowdown and loose ground.
descent: Walk off via the summit ridge and the standard northwest-ridge / base-jumper trail down the west side to the old logging road at the Barclay Lake trailhead.
itinerary: Realistically a full car-to-car day with a very early start, or a two-day outing. Day 1: drive to the Barclay Lake trailhead the night before, hike the 2.2 miles to Barclay Lake in the evening and bivy near the lake (established sites exist; Wild Sky Wilderness rules apply). Day 2: leave camp before first light, brush-bash to the base of the north face, climb the fourteen pitches, top out, and take the northwest-ridge/base-jumper trail all the way down to the trailhead — you will not be returning to a lakeside camp, so carry everything over the top or accept a retrieval walk back in.

name: Infinite Beauty
approach: From Cle Elum, drive WA-903 north about 19 miles to the Salmon La Sac Campground entrance and bear right on the gravel road, not into the campground, about 1/4 mile to the Salmon La Sac Trailhead (~2,500 ft). From the Salmon La Sac Trailhead, follow the Waptus River Trail and PCT about 9 miles to Waptus Lake and on to a camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge, roughly 11-12 flat miles one-way; from camp, the old track along Shovel Creek leads to the base of the Mega Slab, starting at its lowest point.
descent: Downclimb the low-angle slab (reversing the ascent line) or descend toward Shovel Lake.
itinerary: Day 1: backpack in via the Waptus River Trail/PCT to a camp near the Waptus River bridge (~12 mi). Day 2: hike to the lowest point of the Mega Slab, climb the shallow-rib start and merge with Timeless Treasure's line, finish 3 pitches of 5.6+ on the summit block, and descend via Shovel Lake or the ascent line. Day 3: hike out.

name: Southwest Face
approach: From North Bend, take I-90 to exit 34, follow 468th Ave SE north 0.6 mi, then turn right onto Middle Fork Road (FS Road 56). Continue 12 miles (paved becoming rough) to where the road veers right, then drive ~5 more rough, high-clearance-recommended miles to the Dingford Creek Trailhead (~1,500 ft), where the road is gated and the Dutch Miller Gap Trail starts up the old roadbed. Hike the Middle Fork Snoqualmie on the Dutch Miller Gap Trail roughly 15 miles to Dutch Miller Gap, then continue to a camp below the SW Face. Total round-trip trail distance for the outing is about 30 miles, plus the scramble from camp to the summit and back.
descent: Reverse the route: 3 single-rope rappels down the summit block to the notch, then downclimb the Class 3-4 gully system back toward Dutch Miller Gap.
itinerary: Day 1: Drive to the Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead and hike ~15 miles up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap, then continue to a camp below the SW Face. Day 2: Climb the SW Face — ~1,000 ft of gully scrambling then the 3-pitch summit block (~6 hrs camp-to-summit) — and descend via rappels and downclimbing back to camp (~4.7 hrs). Day 3: Hike back out to the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Dingford Creek Trailhead (Dutch Miller Gap Trail)

name: Timeless Treasure
approach: From the Salmon La Sac Trailhead, follow the Waptus River Trail and PCT about 9 miles to Waptus Lake and on to a camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge, roughly 11-12 flat miles one-way. From camp, an old, faint, unmaintained track parallels Shovel Creek through forest to a bench around 3,400 ft, then talus-hops to the base of the Mega Slab (~3,700 ft) near Shovel Creek.
descent: Downclimb the low-angle slab (reversing the ascent line) or descend toward Shovel Lake.
itinerary: Day 1: backpack in via the Waptus River Trail/PCT to a camp near the Waptus River bridge (~12 mi). Day 2: hike the old track along Shovel Creek to the slab base (roughly 4-4.5 hours from the trailhead), climb ~3,000 ft of 4th-class slab to the summit block, finish 3 pitches of 5.6+ to the top, and descend via Shovel Lake or the ascent line. Day 3: hike out.

name: Dry Creek Route
approach: From the Big Four Picnic Area / Ice Caves Trailhead (1,640 ft) on the Mountain Loop Highway, follow the paved nature-trail toward the ice caves, then leave the trail to cross the South Fork Stillaguamish River on a fallen log. Travel southeasterly through open forest roughly a mile to reach Dry Creek, then ascend through the lower basin -- in snow conditions via a hidden snow chute, in bare conditions via a series of class 3-4 ledges and ramps -- into the upper basin. From the upper basin, climb the steep main couloir, then traverse the exposed red slabs to gain the summit ridge.
descent: Reverse the Dry Creek line: from the summit follow the summit ridge back, then rappel (~60m) from a notch on the south ridge before downclimbing steep terrain back into the lower basin.
itinerary: A single long day from the trailhead: hike the approach trail/road to the Dry Creek basin, ascend the ledges, the main couloir and the red-slab traverse to the summit ridge, follow it to the true summit, then reverse via the south-ridge rappel and downclimb back to the basin and trailhead.

waypoints.name: Big Four Picnic Area / Ice Caves Trailhead

name: Spindrift Couloir
approach: Walk the nearly wheelchair-accessible nature trail from the Big Four Picnic Area toward the Ice Caves, to the open basin below the North Face. From the trail's end, move right to find a break in the lower cliffs -- straightforward with adequate snow cover, but may require bushwhacking on the far right in sparse-snow years.
descent: Descend northwest via rappels and steep downclimbing to the col between Big Four and Hall Peak, then continue with tree-anchored rappels down through the north face bowl to the base.

bivy.name: Big Four north-side staging and base bivouac
bivy.notes: Big Four is a car-to-car objective by design: the trailhead sits at low elevation barely a mile from the base of a face that rises about 4,000 feet, so the climbing starts almost immediately and there is no approach worth camping to shorten. Parties on the north-side lines, including the long winter couloir routes, typically leave overnight gear at the base and go up and down in a push rather than carrying a bivouac onto the face, which is a considered choice on a wall this active — rockfall and avalanche off it are constant and audible through the night. That same activity is why this is a contingency and not a recommendation: sleeping under this face means sleeping under a debris cone that is there because things fall on it. Position any bivouac well out of the runout, not at the toe of the snow. The ice caves at the base are lethal and collapse every year — do not camp near them, on them, or in them, and stay off them entirely. The nearest legal drive-in beds are the developed campgrounds down the paved loop toward Verlot.
bivy.water: Creeks draining the face run all season near the base, and the debris field itself is meltwater. Treat everything. There is no developed water at the picnic area.
bivy.permit: Not inside any wilderness — this side of the highway is ordinary national forest with no camping permit requirement. A federal recreation pass is required to park at the picnic area. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer and are frequently forest-wide.
bivy.capacity: No established camp of any kind. The picnic area at the trailhead is day use only and camping there is not permitted; parties climbing the north side bivouac informally at the base of the face on the avalanche debris and boulder ground beyond the maintained path.

itinerary: Typically climbed car-to-car or as a single long push: approach the basin below the North Face, climb the couloir in roughly 9 hours (first-ascent pace) to the summit ridge, then descend northwest via rappels/downclimbing to the Big Four-Hall Peak col and tree-anchored rappels through the bowl.

waypoints.name: Big Four Picnic Area / Ice Caves Trailhead

name: Going Down Under
approach: Same south-face approach as Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully (left fork at the high Y-junction) to the base of the Beckey-Tate start, then traverse right across overlaps to the route's own start ledge.
descent: Descend via the standard notch-and-gully descent used for Beckey-Tate, back to the Hairpin pullout.
itinerary: A full alpine day: multi-hour approach, five pitches of sustained 5.9-5.11c climbing, and a roughly two-hour descent.

name: Kearney-Thomas
approach: Park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20 (roughly Milepost 163, about 1 mile east of Washington Pass). Follow the Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak climbers' path south along Early Winters Creek for roughly 2 miles, then leave the trail to cross the creek and ascend the prominent gully system to the base of the south face, taking the left fork at the high Y-junction. Expect 2.5 to 5 hours of approach time; water is unreliable late season.
descent: Scramble to the notch north of the summit, then descend the loose gully back to the Hairpin pullout (as for Beckey-Tate).
itinerary: A long alpine day: multi-hour approach, 7-8 pitches of sustained 5.9-5.11 climbing, and a roughly two-hour descent; strong parties may do it car-to-car, others bivy to split the effort.

name: Skinny Start
approach: Same south-face approach as Kearney-Thomas/Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully (left fork at the high Y-junction) to the base of the south face, then locate the start about 30 meters right of the standard Kearney-Thomas start.
descent: Intended descent is via the Beckey-Tate gully, though one party looking to rappel the Beckey-Tate line could not locate anchors and instead downclimbed/traversed to a saddle.
itinerary: A long, sustained day: multi-hour approach, three hard pitches that join the Kearney-Thomas finish, and a descent that can run long if you go looking for rappel anchors.

name: Walkabout
approach: Same as Beckey-Tate/Kearney-Thomas: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak path south along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the prominent south-face approach gully (left fork at the high Y-junction). Expect 2.5-5 hours; water is unreliable late season.
descent: Descend via the Beckey-Tate line: scramble to the notch, then the loose gully back to the Hairpin pullout.
itinerary: A serious multi-day undertaking as first climbed: the FA team took three days ground-up, including a summit bivy, before descending via Beckey-Tate the next morning.

name: West Ridge (Standard Route)
approach: Park in a highway pullout on SR-20 about 3.5 miles east of the Washington Pass summit (roughly 4,320 ft elevation). Descend to and cross Early Winters Creek, then head up into the Willow Creek valley, staying on the north side of the creek. The first ~3/4 mile up the valley is steep and can be very brushy in summer. Around 5,000 ft the slope eases; continue up loose/open terrain into the upper basin near 7,000 ft, then traverse a loose scree or snow slope for about 400 ft to reach the saddle on the west ridge (~7,400 ft). Stay left of the waterfall cliff band in the Willow Creek valley; angling right of the creek runs into cliffs. A higher log crossing a few hundred feet upstream of the lowest one keeps your feet drier on Early Winters Creek.
descent: Reverse the route: friction-downclimb and rappel (2 short raps, 30m rope) off the summit block, then descend the class 2 west ridge and scree/basin back into the Willow Creek drainage to the highway.
itinerary: Typically climbed as a single long day car-to-car; parties often return close to sunset given the brushy approach, loose scree, and slow travel. A 2-day/overnight option with a basin bivy is sometimes used, especially when combined with an adjacent objective (e.g., a Silver Star–Big Snagtooth traverse, reported at 12-18 hours).

waypoints.name: SR-20 pullout (Silver Star / Willow Creek approach)

name: East Buttress
approach: Approach as for the East Ridge/Hardscrabble Route: walk/bike the gated Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road to the Hardscrabble Lakes boot path, then continue to lower Hardscrabble Lake. Traverse the lake's left (north) side and scramble two rock bands to reach the buttress's south side at roughly 5,400 ft.
itinerary: A full climbing day: long approach via Hardscrabble Lakes followed by 10 pitches of climbing: plan for an early start and be prepared for a long descent/approach reversal.

name: East Ridge (Hardscrabble) Route
approach: Start at the Dingford Creek Trailhead gate and walk (or mountain-bike) the closed Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road about 7 miles to the boot path for Hardscrabble Lakes, which starts roughly half a mile short of the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, across the road from a large fallen log. Follow the climbers path east through forest to upper Hardscrabble Lake, staying near the inlet — straying left leads into cliff bands. The path from the old road to the lower lake is overgrown but cairned across the talus; fallen trees at each end of the talus make it easy to lose. Above the upper lake expect a brush bash to reach the talus gully, in both directions.
descent: Reverse the east ridge/north-slope line back to the col above Hardscrabble Lakes and down the gully to the lakes, then the long road walk back to the Dingford Creek Trailhead.

bivy.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
bivy.notes: The high camp for Big Snow Mountain's east ridge, which is the easier and much less confusing of that peak's two routes. From the boot path junction on the old road the trail climbs steeply and roughly to lower Hardscrabble Lake at about 4,060 ft, and the upper lake is another half mile and 500 ft above it. The path is a climbers' track, not a maintained trail, and the section between the lakes is slabby, brushy and locally class 3 or 4 — this is the hardest walking on the route. From the upper lake the east ridge route goes over a pass at roughly 5,760 ft and then along to the summit at 6,680 ft, with a final few hundred feet that often want microspikes well into summer. The alternative north slope route from Dingford Creek is shorter on paper and involves serious route-finding and bushwhacking whose difficulty depends entirely on how much snow is still lying; parties who have done both generally recommend the east ridge unless the north side is still filled in. The same camp is the natural start for the high traverse west toward Iron Cap Mountain. Season is essentially August and September; earlier and the slabs below the lakes are running with meltwater. Unlike the Cle Elum-side camps in this zone, the Middle Fork approach was outside the 2026 fire closure — which is the one situation in which the western approach to this range is the correct choice.
bivy.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
bivy.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is gated at Dingford Creek, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. Burnt Boot Peak is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

itinerary: Given the roughly 25-mile round trip created by the Dingford Creek gate closure, this route is typically done as an overnight backpack with a camp at Hardscrabble Lakes; a single-day car-to-car push is possible only for very fit, fast parties, some of whom bike the road-walk sections.

waypoints.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie

name: North Slope (Dingford) Route
approach: Drive to the Dingford Creek Trailhead gate via Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Rd / FSR 56 (about 18 mi from North Bend; the last several miles are rough gravel, high-clearance recommended). Hike the Dingford Creek Trail roughly 3.2 mi to the Hester Lake Trail junction, continue left (east) toward Myrtle Lake (about 2 more miles). From Myrtle Lake, leave the trail and climb steep, increasingly brushy terrain toward Big Snow Lake, then traverse right around Snowflake Lake before ascending gullies/a snow couloir on the mountain's NW flank to the upper rock fields.
descent: Reverse the ascent line back down through the upper rock fields, around Snowflake and Big Snow Lakes, to Myrtle Lake and the Dingford Creek Trail.

bivy.name: Myrtle Lake
bivy.notes: End of the Dingford Creek trail and the usual place to split this route; Big Snow Lake, higher up, has two or three more sites. Many parties do the climb in one long day.
bivy.water: Lake
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: Several established sites around the lake

itinerary: Doable as a long car-to-car day for fit, route-finding-savvy parties (a similar NW-slope trip report logged roughly 6.7 hrs up / 4.8 hrs down, about 11.5 hrs total). Many parties instead backpack in and camp at Myrtle Lake or Big Snow Lake to split the trip over two days.

name: Northeast Ridge
approach: As for the South Ridge: Rainy Pass/Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20, via Heather Pass and Lewis Lake to a camp at Wing Lake (~6,900 ft). From camp, ascend snow (a small permanent snowfield/mini-glacier can persist below the col into September) toward the low point in the Northeast Ridge — following the hogsback moraine wide right and then traversing back left to the notch is reported to stay on more stable ground than a direct line. On fine early-October weekends, larch-season crowds fill the Rainy Pass lots and line the highway shoulder; start early to secure parking.
descent: Descend via the South Ridge/South Route: down-climb or make a short rappel off the ridge to benches below, work south to the south col, then down the loose gully back toward Wing Lake.

bivy.name: Wing Lake
bivy.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Black Peak and the natural first night for Corteo as well. From the Rainy Pass west lot the loop trail is followed for a little over a mile, then a right fork leads to Heather Pass; from there a boot path crosses a boulder field and drops to Lewis Lake, and a further climb of about twelve hundred feet up the northwest slope reaches Wing Lake in the cirque under Black Peak. Reckon on four to six hours with a pack, and four to seven more from camp to summit and back. Camping here rather than at Lewis costs an hour on the way in and buys a much shorter summit day, which matters because everything above is talus and heather with route-finding rather than trail. The boundary detail is worth knowing: Black Peak's summit stands on the line between the forest and the national park, but this camp is on the forest side, so a party sleeping here needs no permit even though it is climbing a peak the park shares.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. Snow patches under Black Peak feed it well into the autumn. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: None. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, not the national park, so there is no backcountry permit, no quota and nothing to reserve. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass covers parking at Rainy Pass. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine from mid summer onward and at this elevation there is almost nothing to burn anyway, so plan on a stove and check the current order rather than assuming a fire is legal.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established pads in the boulders and heather around the outlet, most taking one or two tents. It is the best ground on this side of the peak and it fills on clear summer weekends and hard in larch season, so have Lewis Lake in mind as the fallback.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures
bivy.notes: This is the door to Black Peak and Corteo and the reason both are approachable in a weekend. It is also where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north, so the lots serve two entirely different sets of objectives and are busier than their size suggests. The closures above exist because the loop is one of the most walked trails in the state and its meadows were being trampled; they are enforced rather than advisory. Parties commonly sleep in the car here before an early start, and there is a toilet but no water. Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.
bivy.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
bivy.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.

bivy.name: Lewis Lake
bivy.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. Most parties treat it as a waypoint rather than a destination, but it is a genuine camp and a sensible one for a late start, a heavy pack or a party that wants a shorter first day. It is also where the Corteo approach commits: from here the line follows the top of the moraine onto the Lewis Glacier and climbs southeast, bearing left at the top, to a notch on the ridge near seven thousand five hundred feet, then works west along the ridge and downclimbs several hundred feet of dirt or snow into the cirque under Corteo's west face, gaining the southwest ridge at a large notch by an easy gully. Nothing above Lewis is trail. Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass into early summer and an axe is worth carrying until it has gone.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
bivy.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: A few sites around the shore, fewer and rougher than Wing Lake's. Adequate for a party or two, and the obvious answer when Wing is full or when weather turns on the way up.

itinerary: Commonly done as a 2-3 day trip: Day 1 hike in to Wing Lake camp; Day 2 climb the Northeast Ridge and descend via the South Ridge back to camp (a long day, often 12-17 hrs car-to-camp-to-car for strong parties doing it in one push from the trailhead); Day 3 hike out if camping two nights.

name: Blue's Buttress
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington/Sedro-Woolley, then east on SR-20 through Marblemount and over Rainy Pass and Washington Pass; from Winthrop/Mazama it's a quick 20-30 minute drive west on SR-20 instead. Park in the large pullout at the hairpin turn on SR-20, about a mile east of Washington Pass. Walk south through the boulder field on the climbers' path that heads up the valley toward Kangaroo Pass. After roughly half a mile, leave the path where a drainage comes down off Poster Peak on the right, and follow cairns up it through trees and talus, staying low near treeline rather than traversing high on loose rock, to the foot of Poster Peak's two northeast buttresses. Blue's Buttress is the left-hand (southerly) one, marked by a large roof low down; allow a little over an hour from the car.
descent: Walk southeast off the summit toward the col along the southeast ridge (at approximately 7,130 feet). Descend the steep loose gully back toward the base of the buttresses. Take care on loose terrain and snow-covered sections if present.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
bivy.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
bivy.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

itinerary: Single-day car-to-car outing: drive to the hairpin turnout, hike/scramble the approach to the base of the buttress (~1-1.5 hrs), climb Blue's Buttress via simul-climbing with roped pitches through the crux sections (~2-3 hrs), descend via the SE col and scree gully back to the car (~2 hrs) — typically 5-6 hours round trip.
